---
title: "The Laplace approximation"
execute: {warning: false, message: false}
---

A [generalized linear mixed model](generalized-linear-mixed-models.qmd) contains group deviations that are not observed directly. The response likelihood is conditional on their values, and the model assigns those values a population distribution. Recall that [marginalization](../random-variables-and-distributions/marginal-distributions.qmd) sums or integrates a joint distribution over a quantity we do not observe. A likelihood for the observed responses must thus average over every possible group deviation.

The [group deviation model](fixed-and-random-effects.qmd) defines what is being integrated. Its [standard deviations and covariances](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd) determine how plausible different deviation values are. Recall that the [likelihood](../statistical-inference/maximum-likelihood.qmd) views the density of the realized responses as a function of the population coefficients and group distribution parameters.

The basic idea is to replace a difficult peak with a normal shaped peak whose area we already know how to calculate. We first identify the integral, then construct the local quadratic approximation that produces this normal shape, and finally compare the approximation with direct integration for a restricted SuperTelicity model.

This integral usually has no elementary form for a logistic mixed model. The [**Laplace approximation**](https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1986.10478240) replaces the log integrand with a quadratic near its highest point. We work through that computation with one participant intercept from [SuperTelicity](generalized-linear-mixed-models.qmd).

## Why the integral appears

For participant $p$, let $\mathbf y_p$ denote the binary preposition choices and $b_p$ the participant intercept. Conditional on $b_p$, the participant likelihood is

$$
p(\mathbf y_p\mid b_p,\boldsymbol\beta).
$$

The group model supplies the density $f_B(b_p\mid\tau)$. The contribution from the observed responses is

$$
p(\mathbf y_p\mid\boldsymbol\beta,\tau)
=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
p(\mathbf y_p\mid b_p,\boldsymbol\beta)
f_B(b_p\mid\tau)\,db_p.
$$

Integration adds support over every intercept value. Selecting only the best-fitting intercept would omit uncertainty about that latent value.

Before observation, $\mathbf Y_p$ and $B_p$ are random. After the responses are recorded, $\mathbf y_p$ is fixed in the likelihood while $b$ indexes possible unobserved intercept values. The integrand is explicitly

$$
\underbrace{\prod_i
\pi_i(b)^{y_i}[1-\pi_i(b)]^{1-y_i}}_{\text{Bernoulli likelihood}}
\times
\underbrace{\frac{1}{\tau\sqrt{2\pi}}
\exp\left(-\frac{b^2}{2\tau^2}\right)}_{\text{normal group density}}.
$$

The integral is area. The Laplace approximation estimates that area from two
local features: the integrand's height at its **mode**, the value of \(b\) where
the integrand is highest, and the peak's width. A high but very narrow peak can
thus have less area than a lower, wider peak. We will derive the quantity that
measures that width rather than assume its form.

For intuition, a rectangular peak with height $h$ and width $w$ has area $hw$. Knowing $h$ without $w$ is therefore insufficient. The same fact holds for smooth likelihood peaks: we need both the value at the mode and a measure of how rapidly the function falls away from it.

## Expanding the log integrand

Recall that a [first derivative measures local
change](../random-variables-and-distributions/expected-values.qmd#derivatives-as-local-rates-of-change).
A second derivative measures how that rate of change itself changes, which is
why it describes **curvature**: a large negative second derivative marks a
sharply bending peak, while a value near zero marks a flatter one. The [Hessian
discussion](../statistical-inference/beyond-conjugacy.qmd#hessian-as-local-curvature)
extends this idea to several parameters.

A **Taylor approximation** replaces a smooth function near a chosen point by a
polynomial that has the same value and derivatives there. Keeping terms through
the second derivative gives a local quadratic. We use that quadratic because
exponentiating a downward-opening quadratic produces the shape of a normal
density, whose area we know how to calculate.

To connect that claim to a familiar formula, recall that

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
\exp\left\{-\frac{H}{2}(b-\widehat b)^2\right\}\,db
=\sqrt{\frac{2\pi}{H}}.
$$

The constant $H$ controls width. If $H$ is large, the exponent becomes very negative after a small move from $\widehat b$, so the peak is narrow. If $H$ is small, the peak is wide.

Define

$$
h(b)
=\log p(\mathbf y_p\mid b,\boldsymbol\beta)
+\log f_B(b\mid\tau).
$$

Let $\widehat b$ maximize $h(b)$. At this mode, a small move to either side has
no first-order advantage, so

$$
h'(\widehat b)=0.
$$

The second-order Taylor expansion is

$$
h(b)
\approx h(\widehat b)
+h'(\widehat b)(b-\widehat b)
+\frac{1}{2}h''(\widehat b)(b-\widehat b)^2.
$$

The first-derivative term vanishes at the mode. The second derivative is
negative at an ordinary local maximum, so we write its negative as the positive
curvature magnitude

$$
H=-h''(\widehat b)>0
$$

and obtain

$$
h(b)
\approx h(\widehat b)-\frac{H}{2}(b-\widehat b)^2.
$$

Exponentiating produces a normal-shaped approximation whose integral is

$$
\int \exp\{h(b)\}\,db
\approx
\exp\{h(\widehat b)\}
\sqrt{\frac{2\pi}{H}}.
$$

Equivalently,

$$
\log L
\approx h(\widehat b)
+\frac{1}{2}\log(2\pi)
-\frac{1}{2}\log H.
$$

The height records support at the conditional mode. The curvature records how quickly support falls away from it.

## Constructing the SuperTelicity integrand

The fuller GLMM has participant, verb, and sentence intercepts. To make one integration step directly inspectable, we restrict the worked model to a participant intercept. The comparison therefore studies Laplace error for that one-dimensional integral rather than the complete crossed model.

The code will need the mode and the curvature there. `optimize()` searches a bounded interval for the value of $b$ that minimizes a function, so we give it the negative log integrand to find the maximum of the original log integrand. The curvature calculation also follows directly from the model. For a Bernoulli observation with fitted probability $p_i(b)$, the negative second derivative of its log likelihood with respect to $b$ is $p_i(b)[1-p_i(b)]$. The normal group density contributes $1/\tau^2$. Adding over trials gives

$$
H
=\sum_i p_i(\widehat b)[1-p_i(\widehat b)]
+\frac{1}{\tau^2}.
$$

Thus the code is evaluating the curvature formula derived above rather than asking software for an unexplained quantity.

```{r}
#| label: supertelicity-laplace
library(lme4)
library(ggplot2)

supertelicity <- read.csv("data/supertelicity/supertelicity-cloze.csv")
supertelicity$participant_id <- factor(supertelicity$participant_id)
supertelicity$verb_type <- factor(
  supertelicity$verb_type,
  levels = c("manner", "result")
)
supertelicity$contentfulness <- factor(
  supertelicity$contentfulness,
  levels = c("contentful", "bleached", "templatic")
)
contrasts(supertelicity$verb_type) <- contr.sum(2)
contrasts(supertelicity$contentfulness) <- contr.sum(3)

fit <- glmer(
  prep_in ~ verb_type * contentfulness +
    (1 | participant_id),
  data = supertelicity,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"),
  nAGQ = 1L,
  control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa")
)

participant_sizes <- sort(table(supertelicity$participant_id))
selected_participant <- names(participant_sizes)[
  ceiling(length(participant_sizes) / 2)
]
participant_data <- supertelicity[
  supertelicity$participant_id == selected_participant,
]

fixed_matrix <- model.matrix(
  delete.response(terms(fit, fixed.only = TRUE)),
  participant_data
)
fixed_location <- drop(fixed_matrix %*% fixef(fit))
participant_sd <- attr(
  VarCorr(fit)$participant_id,
  "stddev"
)[[1L]]

log1pexp <- function(x) {
  pmax(x, 0) + log1p(exp(-abs(x)))
}

log_integrand <- function(b) {
  bernoulli_part <- sum(
    participant_data$prep_in * (fixed_location + b) -
      log1pexp(fixed_location + b)
  )
  normal_part <- dnorm(
    b,
    sd = participant_sd,
    log = TRUE
  )
  bernoulli_part + normal_part
}

mode_result <- optimize(
  function(b) -log_integrand(b),
  interval = c(-6 * participant_sd, 6 * participant_sd)
)
conditional_mode <- mode_result$minimum
mode_probability <- plogis(fixed_location + conditional_mode)
curvature <- sum(mode_probability * (1 - mode_probability)) +
  1 / participant_sd^2
```

The selected participant has `r nrow(participant_data)` observed trials. This count and every likelihood quantity below are computed from those responses.

We extend the search interval six fitted random effect standard deviations in each direction, which covers the practically relevant normal density. The participant is selected by median trial count so that the worked curve is not chosen for an unusually sparse or unusually dense response history.

## Comparing the exact integral with its local approximation

Numerical integration is stabilized by subtracting the log integrand at the mode before exponentiation.

That subtraction rescales the largest exponentiated value to one and prevents numerical overflow or underflow. Adding `log_height` back after integration restores the original log integral; it does not alter the mathematical target.

```{r}
#| label: supertelicity-laplace-summary
log_height <- log_integrand(conditional_mode)

centered_integral <- integrate(
  function(b) {
    vapply(
      b,
      function(value) {
        exp(log_integrand(value) - log_height)
      },
      numeric(1)
    )
  },
  lower = -Inf,
  upper = Inf,
  rel.tol = 1e-11
)$value

exact_log_integral <- log(centered_integral) + log_height
laplace_log_integral <- log_height +
  0.5 * log(2 * pi) -
  0.5 * log(curvature)

laplace_summary <- data.frame(
  participant_id = selected_participant,
  trials = nrow(participant_data),
  conditional_mode = conditional_mode,
  negative_second_derivative = curvature,
  exact_log_integral = exact_log_integral,
  laplace_log_integral = laplace_log_integral,
  laplace_minus_exact = laplace_log_integral - exact_log_integral
)
laplace_summary
```

The difference is an empirical computation diagnostic for these observed trials. Accuracy may differ for other participants and for the higher dimensional crossed model.

```{r}
#| label: plot-laplace
intercept_grid <- data.frame(
  participant_intercept = seq(
    conditional_mode - 4 / sqrt(curvature),
    conditional_mode + 4 / sqrt(curvature),
    length.out = 240L
  )
)
intercept_grid$exact <- vapply(
  intercept_grid$participant_intercept,
  log_integrand,
  numeric(1)
) - log_height
intercept_grid$quadratic <- -0.5 * curvature *
  (intercept_grid$participant_intercept - conditional_mode)^2

plot_data <- rbind(
  data.frame(
    participant_intercept = intercept_grid$participant_intercept,
    relative_log_integrand = intercept_grid$exact,
    curve = "Exact log integrand"
  ),
  data.frame(
    participant_intercept = intercept_grid$participant_intercept,
    relative_log_integrand = intercept_grid$quadratic,
    curve = "Local quadratic"
  )
)

ggplot(
  plot_data,
  aes(
    x = participant_intercept,
    y = relative_log_integrand,
    linetype = curve
  )
) +
  geom_line(color = "#1F5A85", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(
    x = "Participant random intercept",
    y = "Log integrand relative to its mode",
    linetype = NULL
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

The approximation changes how we evaluate the integral; it leaves the response
model unchanged. It cannot add a predictor, repair a missing random slope, or
make an inappropriate link valid. It tends to be most accurate when the
integrand is concentrated and roughly symmetric near its mode; sparse groups,
rare responses, boundary variances, or strong asymmetry may make the local
quadratic less adequate.

In `glmer`, `nAGQ = 1` selects this one-point Laplace calculation. The one-intercept restriction exists only to expose it in one dimension. In the crossed participant, verb, and sentence model, the integral is high-dimensional and can be skewed or weakly concentrated along some covariance directions. Agreement in the selected one-dimensional example thus cannot guarantee equal accuracy in that fitted crossed model.

## Recap and check

1. Why not insert only $\widehat b$ into the conditional likelihood? Doing so retains peak height but discards the width that represents uncertainty over possible random effect values.
2. What does subtracting `log_height` change? Only numerical scale; the value is added back on the log scale after integration.
3. Does `nAGQ = 1` change the Bernoulli response model? No. It chooses an approximation for the same random effect integral.

The tools for [model criticism and prediction](../model-criticism-and-prediction/) ask whether a computationally successful fit still gives an inadequate account of the data.
